types.concept: Conceptual: principles, models, how things relate and why
types.decision: Conditional: when and why to apply which knowledge
types.prior: Assumed prior knowledge, not taught in this chapter

schema.relation_semantics: prereq: B lists A in 'prereq' when A must be mastered before B. 'links' are semantic relations (from, rel, to).

bigIdeas.name: Prior knowledge
bigIdeas.summary: Physics and thermodynamics the chapter assumes but does not teach.

bigIdeas.name: Thrust from momentum
bigIdeas.summary: Every jet engine makes thrust by accelerating air rearward; the thrust equation quantifies it.

bigIdeas.name: Turbojet anatomy
bigIdeas.summary: Five sections in flow order, each with one job; the turbine powers the compressor.

bigIdeas.name: Brayton cycle & thermal efficiency
bigIdeas.summary: The ideal four-process cycle; efficiency depends only on pressure ratio and γ.

bigIdeas.name: Propulsive efficiency & engine families
bigIdeas.summary: Large mass flow at small velocity increment wastes less energy; this explains which architecture fits which flight regime.

kcs.name: Newton's laws of motion
kcs.objective: Can state Newton's third law and apply it to a force pair.

kcs.name: Momentum conservation & control volumes
kcs.objective: Can apply conservation of linear momentum to a control volume with mass flowing in and out.

kcs.name: Ideal gas, isentropic processes, entropy
kcs.objective: Can describe adiabatic/reversible (isentropic) and constant-pressure processes of an ideal gas.

kcs.name: Kinetic energy & power
kcs.objective: Can use KE = ½mv², power = force × velocity, and their per-second (mass-flow) forms.

kcs.name: Mach number & compressibility
kcs.objective: Can explain what subsonic, transonic and supersonic mean and why compressibility losses appear near Mach 1.

kcs.name: Newton's 3rd law as the jet principle
kcs.objective: Can explain how accelerating air rearward pushes the engine forward.
kcs.explain: The engine accelerates a mass of air (plus burned-fuel products) rearward. By Newton's third law the engine is pushed forward. This single principle applies to every jet engine, whatever its size or layout.
misconceptions: Thinking the exhaust 'pushes against the outside air'. The force comes from accelerating the air through the engine.

items.q: What single physical principle underlies every jet engine, and how does it produce a forward force?
items.a: Newton's third law. The engine accelerates air (and fuel products) rearward; the reaction force pushes the engine forward.

kcs.name: Definition of thrust
kcs.objective: Can define thrust precisely.
kcs.explain: Thrust (F) is the net forward force produced by the momentum exchange between the engine and its working fluid.

items.q: Define thrust.
items.a: The net forward force resulting from momentum exchange with the working fluid.

kcs.name: Jet vs. propeller thrust generation
kcs.objective: Can contrast how a jet engine and a propeller generate thrust.
kcs.explain: A propeller relies mainly on an external airfoil producing a pressure difference. A jet engine generates thrust entirely by processing air internally: draw in, compress, energize, expel at high velocity.

items.q: How does thrust generation in a jet engine differ from a propeller aircraft?
items.a: The propeller relies mainly on an external airfoil creating a pressure difference. The jet processes air internally: intake, compression, energizing (combustion), expulsion at high velocity.

kcs.name: General thrust equation
kcs.objective: Can write the full thrust equation, name every symbol and state where it comes from.
kcs.explain: Derived from conservation of linear momentum on a control volume around the engine. ṁa = air mass flow rate; Ve = exhaust velocity; V0 = flight (freestream) velocity; pe, p0 = exhaust and ambient static pressure; Ae = nozzle exit area. First term: momentum thrust. Second term: pressure thrust.
misconceptions: Using Ve instead of (Ve − V0). In flight the incoming air already moves at V0 relative to the engine.

items.q: Write the general net thrust equation and name every symbol.
items.a: F = ṁa(Ve − V0) + (pe − p0)Ae. ṁa: air mass flow; Ve: exhaust velocity; V0: flight velocity; pe/p0: exhaust/ambient static pressure; Ae: nozzle exit area.

items.q: From which conservation law, applied to what, is the thrust equation derived?
items.a: Conservation of linear momentum, applied to a control volume surrounding the engine.

kcs.name: Perfectly expanded nozzle simplification
kcs.objective: Can decide when the pressure term may be dropped and state the remaining momentum form.
kcs.explain: A nozzle is perfectly expanded when exhaust static pressure equals ambient pressure. The pressure term then vanishes. If pe ≠ p0, the pressure term must stay in.
misconceptions: Always dropping the pressure term. Check first that the problem states or implies pe = p0.

items.q: Under what condition may you drop the pressure term, and what equation remains?
items.a: When the nozzle is perfectly expanded (pe = p0). Remaining: F = ṁa(Ve − V0).

kcs.name: Compute net thrust
kcs.objective: Can calculate net thrust from mass flow and velocities, with units.
kcs.explain: Check the nozzle condition, subtract V0 from Ve, multiply by ṁa. kg/s × m/s = N.
misconceptions: Setting V0 = 0 for an aircraft in flight.
Forgetting the unit check: (kg/s)(m/s) = kg·m/s² = N.

items.q: ṁa = 80 kg/s, V0 = 230 m/s, Ve = 480 m/s, perfectly expanded nozzle. Net thrust?
ṁa = 400 kg/s, V0 = 250 m/s, Ve = 320 m/s, perfectly expanded. Net thrust?

kcs.name: Propulsive power = F × V0
kcs.objective: Can compute the propulsive power delivered to the aircraft.
kcs.explain: Useful (thrust) power is thrust times flight speed. It uses V0, not Ve.
misconceptions: Multiplying by Ve. The aircraft moves at V0, so useful power is F × V0.

items.q: An engine produces 15 kN of thrust at a flight speed of 220 m/s. Propulsive power?

kcs.name: Sanity-check a thrust result
kcs.objective: Can convert N ↔ lbf and judge whether a thrust value is plausible.
kcs.explain: 1 lbf ≈ 4.448 N (not given in the chapter). 28 kN ≈ 6,300 lbf, a typical value for one engine of a modern narrow-body regional aircraft.

items.q: Convert 28 kN to lbf. Is it plausible for one engine of a regional narrow-body?
items.a: 28,000 / 4.448 ≈ 6,300 lbf. Yes, that sits in the typical range.

kcs.name: Five turbojet sections in flow order
kcs.objective: Can name the five sections of a turbojet in flow order and sketch them.
kcs.explain: Inlet → compressor → combustor → turbine → nozzle. Compressor and turbine share a common shaft.

items.q: Name the five sections of a turbojet in flow order.
items.a: Inlet, compressor, combustor, turbine, nozzle.

kcs.name: Inlet: slow and diffuse the flow
kcs.objective: Can state the function of the inlet.
kcs.explain: The inlet slows down and diffuses the incoming air before it reaches the compressor.

items.q: What does the inlet do to the incoming air?
items.a: Slows and diffuses it before it reaches the compressor.

kcs.name: Compressor: rotor/stator rows, ×15–40
kcs.objective: Can describe compressor construction and typical modern pressure rise.
kcs.explain: Many rows of rotating (rotor) and stationary (stator) airfoils progressively raise the air pressure, typically by a factor of 15 to 40 in a modern engine.

items.q: How is a compressor built, and by what factor does a modern one raise pressure?
items.a: Many rows of rotor and stator blades; pressure rises progressively by a factor of about 15–40.

kcs.name: Combustor: continuous burning, 1800–2000 K
kcs.objective: Can describe what happens in the combustor and the gas temperatures reached.
kcs.explain: Fuel is injected and burned continuously in the high-pressure air, raising gas temperature to about 1800–2000 K.

items.q: What happens in the combustor, and what gas temperature range is reached?
items.a: Fuel is injected and burned continuously; gas temperature rises to about 1800–2000 K.

kcs.name: Turbine drives the compressor
kcs.objective: Can explain how much work the turbojet turbine extracts and why.
kcs.explain: The turbine extracts just enough mechanical work to drive the compressor through a common shaft. The remaining gas energy goes to the nozzle.
misconceptions: Thinking the turbine produces the thrust. In a turbojet it only powers the compressor; the nozzle produces the jet.

items.q: In a turbojet, how much work does the turbine extract, and for what?
items.a: Just enough to drive the compressor via the common shaft. The rest of the energy is left for the nozzle.

kcs.name: Nozzle: energy → high-velocity jet
kcs.objective: Can state the function of the nozzle.
kcs.explain: The nozzle converts the remaining gas energy into a high-velocity exhaust, which produces thrust.

items.q: What is the nozzle's job?
items.a: Convert the remaining gas energy into high-velocity exhaust, producing thrust.

kcs.name: Brayton (Joule) cycle as the ideal model
kcs.objective: Can state what the Brayton cycle models and its key assumption.
kcs.explain: The Brayton cycle (also Joule cycle) idealizes every gas-turbine engine as four processes performed on air treated as an ideal gas.

items.q: What is the Brayton cycle, what is its other name, and what is the working-fluid assumption?
items.a: The ideal thermodynamic cycle of gas-turbine engines; also called the Joule cycle; air is treated as an ideal gas; four processes.

kcs.name: 1→2 Isentropic compression
kcs.objective: Can describe process 1→2: where it happens and how p, T and s change.
kcs.explain: In the compressor, air is compressed adiabatically and reversibly. Pressure and temperature rise; entropy stays constant.
misconceptions: Confusing isentropic with isothermal. Temperature rises during isentropic compression.

items.q: Describe process 1→2: name, location, and what happens to p, T and s.
items.a: Isentropic compression in the compressor; p and T rise; s stays constant.

kcs.name: 2→3 Constant-pressure heat addition
kcs.objective: Can describe process 2→3.
kcs.explain: In the combustor, burning fuel adds heat at (ideally) constant pressure, sharply increasing temperature.

items.q: Describe process 2→3.
items.a: Constant-pressure heat addition in the combustor; temperature rises sharply.

kcs.name: 3→4 Isentropic expansion
kcs.objective: Can describe process 3→4 and the energy conversions in it.
kcs.explain: The hot gas expands through turbine and nozzle, converting thermal and pressure energy into mechanical work and kinetic energy.

items.q: Describe process 3→4 and the energy conversions.
items.a: Isentropic expansion through turbine and nozzle; thermal + pressure energy become mechanical work (turbine) and kinetic energy (jet).

kcs.name: 4→1 Constant-pressure heat rejection
kcs.objective: Can describe process 4→1 and why it is 'imagined'.
kcs.explain: In the idealized closed cycle the exhaust gas rejects heat to the atmosphere at constant pressure, returning to state 1. A real engine is an open cycle: this step happens outside the engine.
misconceptions: Thinking 4→1 happens inside the engine. It is an idealization closing the cycle in the atmosphere.

items.q: Describe process 4→1. Why is it called imagined?
items.a: Constant-pressure heat rejection to the atmosphere, returning to state 1. Real engines are open cycles; the exhaust leaves, so the step is an idealization.

kcs.name: Map cycle processes ↔ engine components
kcs.objective: Can assign each Brayton process to the engine section where it occurs.
kcs.explain: 1→2 compressor; 2→3 combustor; 3→4 turbine + nozzle; 4→1 atmosphere (idealized). This links BI2 and BI3.

items.q: Match: compressor, combustor, turbine + nozzle, atmosphere → Brayton processes.
items.a: Compressor: 1→2; combustor: 2→3; turbine + nozzle: 3→4; atmosphere: 4→1.

kcs.name: Reading P–v and T–s diagrams
kcs.objective: Can sketch the cycle in P–v and T–s coordinates and interpret the enclosed areas.
kcs.explain: P–v: enclosed area = net specific work output. T–s: enclosed area = net heat converted to work. Isentropic processes (1→2, 3→4) are vertical lines on T–s; constant-pressure processes are horizontal on P–v.
misconceptions: Swapping the meanings of the two enclosed areas.

items.q: Which diagram's enclosed area is net specific work, and which is net heat converted to work?
items.a: P–v: net specific work output. T–s: net heat converted to work.

items.q: On the T–s diagram, which processes appear as vertical lines, and why?
items.a: 1→2 and 3→4, because they are isentropic (constant s).

kcs.name: Pressure ratio rp
kcs.objective: Can define the pressure ratio.
kcs.explain: Ratio of compressor exit to compressor inlet (stagnation) pressure.

items.q: Define the pressure ratio rp.
items.a: rp = p2/p1: compressor exit pressure divided by compressor inlet pressure (stagnation).

kcs.name: Ratio of specific heats γ
kcs.objective: Can state what γ is and its value for air.
kcs.explain: γ = cp/cv; for air γ ≈ 1.4, so (γ − 1)/γ ≈ 0.2857.

items.q: What is γ, and what value is used for air? What is (γ−1)/γ then?
items.a: Ratio of specific heats cp/cv; 1.4 for air; (γ−1)/γ ≈ 0.2857.

kcs.name: Definition of thermal efficiency
kcs.objective: Can define thermal efficiency.
kcs.explain: Fraction of the fuel's heat energy converted into useful shaft or jet work.

items.q: Define thermal efficiency.
items.a: The fraction of fuel heat energy converted into useful shaft or jet work.

kcs.name: Ideal Brayton efficiency formula
kcs.objective: Can write the formula and state that it depends only on rp and γ.
kcs.explain: Ideal thermal efficiency depends only on pressure ratio and γ. Raising rp raises efficiency.
misconceptions: Forgetting the reciprocal (computing 1 − rp^0.2857, which is negative).
Thinking turbine inlet temperature appears in the ideal formula. It does not.

items.q: Write the ideal Brayton thermal efficiency. Which two quantities does it depend on?
items.a: ηth = 1 − 1/rp^((γ−1)/γ). Only on pressure ratio rp and γ.

kcs.name: Compute ideal thermal efficiency
kcs.objective: Can calculate ηth for a given rp and γ.
kcs.explain: Compute the exponent (γ−1)/γ, raise 1/rp to it, subtract from 1. Erratum: the chapter's Exercise 7.1 states (1/12)^0.2857 ≈ 0.535 → 46.5%. The correct value is 0.492 → ηth ≈ 50.8%.
misconceptions: Arithmetic slips with the fractional exponent. Even the textbook's own solution to Ex. 7.1 contains one.

items.q: rp = 12, γ = 1.4. Ideal thermal efficiency?
items.a: (1/12)^0.2857 = 0.492 → ηth ≈ 0.508 = 50.8%. (The chapter's printed 46.5% is wrong.)

items.q: rp = 40, γ = 1.4. Ideal thermal efficiency?

kcs.name: Rising pressure ratios in history
kcs.objective: Can explain the historical rise in pressure ratio and give the milestone values.
kcs.explain: Because ηth rises with rp, raising the compressor's overall pressure ratio is one of the most direct ways to cut fuel use. 1940s turbojets: ≈4:1. Modern high-bypass turbofans: >40:1. Next generation: >50:1.

items.q: Why have compressor pressure ratios grown over time? Give the three milestone values.
items.a: Higher rp directly increases thermal efficiency, i.e. fuel efficiency. ≈4:1 (1940s), >40:1 (modern high-bypass), >50:1 (next generation).

kcs.name: Definition of propulsive efficiency
kcs.objective: Can define propulsive efficiency.
kcs.explain: Fraction of the kinetic energy given to the exhaust that becomes useful thrust power (F × V0).

items.q: Define propulsive efficiency.
items.a: The fraction of the kinetic energy imparted to the exhaust that is converted into useful thrust power.

kcs.name: Large mass, small ΔV principle
kcs.objective: Can explain why propulsive efficiency peaks when Ve is only slightly above V0.
kcs.explain: Thrust ∝ ṁ·ΔV, but kinetic energy left in the jet ∝ ṁ·ΔV². For a required thrust, accelerating a large mass by a small ΔV leaves far less wasted energy than a small mass by a large ΔV. So propulsive power for given thrust is minimized when Ve is close to V0.
misconceptions: 'Higher exhaust velocity means a better engine.' Same thrust can be made with lower Ve and higher ṁ, at higher efficiency.

items.q: Why is propulsive efficiency highest when Ve is only slightly greater than V0?
items.a: Thrust scales with ΔV, but wasted jet kinetic energy scales with ΔV². For a given thrust, using more mass and a smaller ΔV leaves less residual kinetic energy.

items.q: Engine A: ṁ = 100 kg/s, ΔV = 200 m/s. Engine B: ṁ = 400 kg/s, ΔV = 50 m/s. Compare thrust and wasted kinetic power (½ṁΔV²).
items.a: Both 20 kN. Wasted: A = ½·100·200² = 2.0 MW; B = ½·400·50² = 0.5 MW. B wastes 4× less.

kcs.name: Thermal vs. propulsive efficiency
kcs.objective: Can tell which efficiency a design change affects.
kcs.explain: Thermal efficiency: how well fuel heat becomes work (driven by rp). Propulsive efficiency: how well jet kinetic energy becomes thrust power (driven by Ve vs. V0, i.e. bypass). They are improved by different design levers.
misconceptions: Treating 'efficiency' as one number. Pressure ratio raises thermal; bypass raises propulsive.

items.q: Which efficiency improves if (a) the pressure ratio rises from 30 to 45, (b) the bypass ratio rises from 5 to 10?
items.a: (a) Thermal efficiency. (b) Propulsive efficiency.

kcs.name: Turbojet characteristics
kcs.objective: Can characterize the turbojet's exhaust and best flight regime.
kcs.explain: All air passes through compressor, combustor and turbine to one nozzle. High-velocity, low-mass-flow exhaust: excellent at supersonic speeds, poor fuel efficiency at subsonic airliner cruise.

items.q: Characterize a turbojet's exhaust and say where it performs well and badly.
items.a: All air through the core; high Ve, low ṁ. Good at supersonic speeds, poor fuel efficiency at subsonic cruise.

kcs.name: Turbofan characteristics
kcs.objective: Can describe the turbofan and explain why it dominates commercial aviation.
kcs.explain: A large fan ahead of (or integrated with) the compressor; most fan air bypasses the core and exits mixed or through a separate cold nozzle. Larger mass at lower velocity → higher propulsive efficiency → dominant for airliners.
misconceptions: Lower exhaust velocity means less thrust. The larger mass flow compensates.

items.q: How does a turbofan differ from a turbojet, and why does it dominate commercial aviation?
items.a: A fan drives a large bypass flow around the core. It accelerates more mass to lower velocity, which raises propulsive efficiency at subsonic cruise.

kcs.name: Bypass ratio
kcs.objective: Can define bypass ratio and use it to split mass flows.
kcs.explain: Ratio of fan-bypass mass flow to core mass flow in a turbofan.

items.q: Define bypass ratio. A turbofan has BPR 8:1 and core flow 50 kg/s: bypass and total flow?
items.a: Bypass mass flow / core mass flow. Bypass 400 kg/s; total 450 kg/s.

kcs.name: Turboprop & turboshaft
kcs.objective: Can explain where the energy goes and why efficiency drops near transonic speeds.
kcs.explain: The turbine extracts nearly all gas energy and drives a propeller (turboprop) or rotor (turboshaft) through a reduction gearbox. Highest propulsive efficiency at low subsonic speeds; falls sharply toward transonic speeds because propeller tips suffer compressibility losses.
misconceptions: Assuming turboprops are best at all speeds.

items.q: In a turboprop, where does the gas energy go? Why does efficiency drop near transonic flight?
items.a: The turbine extracts nearly all of it to drive the propeller via a reduction gearbox. Near transonic speeds, propeller blade tips meet compressibility losses.

kcs.name: Ramjet
kcs.objective: Can explain ramjet compression and its operating limits.
kcs.explain: No rotating machinery. At high speed the vehicle's forward motion compresses incoming air enough for combustion; a fixed nozzle expands it. No static thrust; viable only above about Mach 1; used for missiles and high-speed research vehicles.
misconceptions: Thinking a ramjet can take off by itself. It produces no static thrust.

items.q: How does a ramjet compress air, and why can it not take off on its own?
items.a: Ram compression from the vehicle's forward speed (no compressor). At zero speed there is no compression, so no static thrust; it needs roughly Mach 1 or more.

kcs.name: Choose engine type for a flight regime
kcs.objective: Can select and justify the right architecture for a given mission.
kcs.explain: Low subsonic: turboprop. High subsonic cruise: turbofan. Supersonic: turbojet. Above ≈ Mach 1 with boost to start: ramjet. Rotorcraft: turboshaft. Fig. 7.3 compares them qualitatively (illustrative values).

items.q: Pick the engine type: (a) long-haul airliner at Mach 0.8, (b) short-haul commuter at 500 km/h, (c) missile at Mach 3, (d) helicopter.
items.a: (a) Turbofan, (b) turboprop, (c) ramjet, (d) turboshaft.
